title: Quadratics Part 2
lead: Part 1 gave you the three forms and factoring. This class covers every other way to solve a quadratic: square roots, the quadratic formula, completing the square and graphing. It also covers the discriminant and the systems where a line meets a parabola. The hard part of these questions is rarely the arithmetic. It is seeing quickly which method the equation is asking for.

parts.title: Part 1 · Choosing a method
parts.html:
First write the equation as ax² + bx + c = 0, then decide:

What you see or what is askedMethod
Small whole numbers or a familiar patternFactor (Class 9)
A squared bracket already alone, such as (x − 2)² = 25Take square roots
Factoring is not obvious, or the answers contain a rootQuadratic formula
The vertex, a minimum or a maximum is askedComplete the square
“How many real solutions?”Discriminant only
Intercepts, intersections or a vertex as numbersGraph it in Desmos

Before you answer, check what was asked. It may be a sum or product of solutions, a coordinate or the value of a constant, not x.

parts.title: Part 2 · Square roots and the quadratic formula
parts.html:
Square roots. When a squared expression is alone on one side, take the square root of both sides and keep both signs.

(x−2)2=25 x−2=5 or x−2=−5 → x=7 or x=−3

The quadratic formula solves every equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0. It is not on the reference sheet, so memorize it.

x=−b±b2−4ac2a
3x2+5x−1=0 a=3, b=5, c=−1
x=−5±52−4(3)(−1)2·3
x=−5±25+126=−5±376

Put negative values in brackets when you substitute; that is where the sign errors come from. A root such as √37 in the answer tells you factoring would never have worked.

The formula is reliable but not always the quickest. For x² − 49 = 0, the difference of squares gives (x − 7)(x + 7) = 0 at once.

parts.title: Part 3 · The discriminant
parts.html:
For ax² + bx + c = 0, the expression b² − 4ac is the discriminant. It tells you how many real solutions there are without solving anything.

b² − 4acReal solutionsPicture
PositiveTwoThe parabola crosses the x-axis twice
ZeroExactly oneThe vertex sits on the x-axis
NegativeNoneThe parabola never reaches the x-axis

The discriminant counts crossings. The vertex-on-the-axis case is the boundary between crossing twice and not at all.

Classic question. x2+kx+9=0 has exactly one real solution. What is a possible value of k? Set the discriminant to zero: k2−4(1)(9)=0 → k2=36 → k=6 or k=−6

The test often asks for one possible value. The negative k is the answer students forget, because they stop at the first square root.

Common mistake. Sign slips in b² − 4ac. Write it out in full before computing. For 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0: (−5)² − 4(2)(3) = 25 − 24 = 1. The square removes the sign of b. When c is negative, the last term turns positive: for 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0 it is 25 − 4(2)(−3) = 25 + 24 = 49.

If a question only asks how many real solutions there are, stop once you have the discriminant. There is no need to finish the formula.

parts.title: Part 4 · Completing the square
parts.html:
Completing the square rewrites x² + bx + constant as a squared term plus a leftover. It is the tool for reaching vertex form and for “what is the minimum value” questions.

The method for x² + bx: take half of b, square it, add it and subtract it.

x2+6x+2 Half of 6 is 3, squared is 9
(x2+6x+9)−9+2=(x+3)2−7
Vertex: (−3,−7)

The −9 + 2 step is where errors happen. You added 9 inside the brackets, so you must subtract 9 to keep the value the same.

Why it works. (x + h)² expands to x² + 2hx + h². The middle coefficient is twice h, so h = b/2 and the square you need is h². Knowing this, a fraction does not stop you: x² + 3x needs (3/2)² = 9/4.

Vertex and minimum or maximum questions. f(x) = x² − 8x + 10 = (x − 4)² − 6. Since (x − 4)² is never negative, the smallest value of f is −6, at x = 4. “What is the minimum value of the function” wants k, not the x-coordinate. Read which one is asked.

Equivalent-expression questions. “Which expression is equivalent to x² + 6x + 2?” with choices in completed-square form. Same computation; the test is checking your bookkeeping.

Solving by completing the square. Move the constant across, add the square to both sides, then take both square roots.

x2+8x−3=0 Move the constant → x2+8x=3
Half of 8 is 4, squared is 16; add 16 to both sides → x2+8x+16=19
(x+4)2=19 → x+4=±19 → x=−4±19

Leaving out the ± loses one of the two solutions. If the coefficient of x² is not 1, divide every term by it first: 3x² + 12x − 6 = 0 becomes x² + 4x − 2 = 0.

parts.title: Part 5 · The vertex and axis of symmetry
parts.html:
Two formulas to memorize. Neither is on the reference sheet.

Axis of symmetry: x=−b2a
Vertex: (−b2a,f(−b2a))

The symmetry rule from Class 9 still earns points: the vertex sits midway between any two points of equal height, and midway between the two roots. If f(1) = f(7), the axis is x = 4. Since the axis is also −b/2a, you get a relation between a and b for free. Hard Module 2 questions chain exactly this: they give f(p) = f(q) and ask for a coefficient.

parts.title: Part 6 · When a line meets a parabola
parts.html:
A line and a parabola can cross twice, touch once, or miss each other. A solution of the system is a point that lies on both graphs, so the number of solutions is the number of shared points.

Algebraic method

  1. Substitute the line (y = mx + b) into the quadratic (y = ax² + cx + d).
  2. Move everything to one side so the equation equals 0. You now have a single quadratic.
  3. To count the intersections, check the discriminant of this new quadratic. To find them, solve it and put each x into the line to get its y.
DiscriminantIntersection points
Positive2
Zero1 (the line is tangent to the curve)
Negative0
The line y=2x−1 intersects the parabola y=x2−4 at how many points? Substitute: x2−4=2x−1 → x2−2x−3=0
Discriminant: (−2)2−4(1)(−3)=16 → positive → two points
Factoring confirms it: (x−3)(x+1)=0 → x=3 or x=−1
Use the line for y: (3,5) and (−1,−3)
The line y=2x+k is tangent to the parabola y=x2. What is k? Substitute: x2=2x+k → x2−2x−k=0
Tangent means discriminant =0: (−2)2−4(1)(−k)=4+4k=0 → k=−1

“How many intersection points” is “how many real solutions does the combined equation have”. A nonlinear system is a quadratic with a second equation attached. The same idea answers “at how many points does the parabola intersect the x-axis?”, which is the discriminant of the quadratic itself.

Desmos method. Type both equations exactly as they are. The number of times the shapes cross is the number of real solutions. If the question asks for coordinates, click the intersection points to read the (x, y) values.

Finding the points. When both equations say y = …, set the two right sides equal. Solve for x, then go back to the line for each y.

y=x+1 and y=x2−3x+1 Set them equal → x+1=x2−3x+1
Move everything to one side → x2−4x=0
Factor → x(x−4)=0 → x=0 or x=4
Use the line: x=0 gives y=1, x=4 gives y=5
Solutions: (0,1) and (4,5)

Four traps.

  • Dropping the second solution. A quadratic usually has two roots. If you find one and stop, you lose a whole intersection point.
  • Stopping at x. A solution of a system is a pair (x, y). Go back to one of the original equations for each y, and use brackets when you substitute a negative number.
  • Mixing up the pairs. Keep each y with the x that produced it. From the example above, (0, 5) is not a solution of either equation.
  • Trusting the graph window. An intersection can sit outside the part of the graph you see. Zoom out, check the scale, and compare the picture with what the discriminant predicts.

Read the last sentence of the question carefully. It may want one coordinate, the sum of the x-values, an ordered pair, or only the number of intersections.

parts.title: Part 7 · The Desmos workflow for hard questions
parts.html:
• One real solution: graph y = (left side) and y = (right side) as separate expressions. Exactly one solution shows as the line resting tangent to the parabola. To test a constant, define it as a slider and watch the tangency appear at the right value.
  • Minimum or maximum value: graph the function and click the vertex. Read both coordinates, then decide which one the question wants.
  • Unknown coefficient: define the function with the unknown as a slider, add the given condition (a plotted point, a root, a value such as f(3) = 10) and slide until it is met. Then verify by substitution, because slider positions are approximate.
  • Equivalent expressions: graph the original and each choice. The equivalent one draws the identical curve. Slower than completing the square for simple cases, but reliable when the expansion gets messy.

Graphing is best when the arithmetic is messy or the choices are numbers. It helps less when the question wants an exact expression, such as a rewritten form or an answer with a root in it.

parts.title: Part 8 · Sum and product of the solutions
parts.html:
For ax² + bx + c = 0, two facts give answers without solving:

QuantityFormula
Sum of the solutions−b / a
Product of the solutionsc / a
2x² − 7x − 15 = 0. What are the sum and the product of the solutions? Sum: −(−7)2=72
Product: −152
Check by factoring: (2x+3)(x−5)=0 → x=−32 or x=5 → sum 72, product −152

Put the equation in the form … = 0 first. For x² + 7x + 19 = 28 − 5x, move everything to the left before reading off a, b and c.

The vertex from factored form. The vertex lies halfway between the two roots. For f(x) = −3(x − 2)(x − 10), the roots are 2 and 10, so the maximum is at x = 6. There is no need to expand.

A fractional root and its factor. A root of 3/2 comes from the factor (2x − 3), which is the same as 2(x − 3/2). When the choices show factors with whole numbers, test each by asking which value of x makes it zero.

“Least value of the constant” with the discriminant.

3x² + 12x + c = 0 has no real solution, and c is an integer. What is the least possible value of c? No real solution → discriminant below zero
122−4(3)(c)<0 → 144−12c<0 → c>12
Least integer: 13

The trap choice is 12, which makes the discriminant exactly zero: one solution, not none.
